why: Multiplying by a constant multiplies both the mean (new mean = 20) and the SD by that constant: new SD = 3 × 2 = 6.

optWhy.A: 3 is the old SD, unchanged (incorrect for multiplication).
optWhy.B: 9 would be the new variance (SD² = 36 → wait; actually 3×3=9 is not variance here).
optWhy.C: 12 would be 3×4.
optWhy.D: Correct. New SD = 3 × 2 = 6.

stem: Classes 0–10 (f=3, mid=5), 10–20 (f=7, mid=15), 20–30 (f=5, mid=25). The grouped mean is:

optWhy.A: 20 is a midpoint, not the mean.
optWhy.B: 18 is not the grouped mean.
optWhy.D: 15 is Σf, not the mean.

stem: Classes 0–10(f=2), 10–20(f=5), 20–30(f=8), 30–40(f=3). n=18. The grouped median is:
why: n/2 = 9. Cumulative frequencies: 2, 7, 15, 18. Median class = 20–30 (L=20, cf=7, f=8, h=10). Median = 20 + (9−7)/8 × 10 = 20 + 2.5 = 22.5.

optWhy.A: 25 is a midpoint, not the median.
optWhy.B: 27.5 is not the median.
optWhy.C: 20 is the lower boundary, not the median.
optWhy.D: Correct. Median = 20 + (2/8)×10 = 22.5.

stem: Group 1: n=10, mean=20. Group 2: n=15, mean=30. The combined mean is:

optWhy.A: 25 is the unweighted mean of 20 and 30, ignoring group sizes.
optWhy.C: 30 is group 2's mean.
optWhy.D: 28 is not the combined mean.

stem: For a positively skewed variable such as annual income, the most appropriate measure of central tendency is:
why: In a positively skewed distribution, extreme high values pull the mean upward. The median is less affected by extreme values and is therefore more appropriate for skewed variables like income.

optWhy.A: The mean is distorted by extreme high values in positive skew.
optWhy.B: Correct. The median is robust to extreme values in skewed distributions.
optWhy.C: The mode is not the best measure of central tendency for income.
optWhy.D: The weighted mean is still affected by extreme values.

stem: Which statement is descriptive rather than inferential?

options.text: The mean anxiety score of this sample is 25.
The population mean anxiety is likely 25.
There is a significant difference between groups.
The result generalises to the population.

why: Descriptive statistics summarise the data at hand (the sample mean is 25). Inferential statistics generalise beyond the sample to the population (options B, C, D).

optWhy.A: Correct. Reporting the sample mean is descriptive.
optWhy.B: Generalising to the population mean is inferential.
optWhy.C: A significant difference between groups is an inferential conclusion.
optWhy.D: Generalising to the population is inferential.

stem: The standard error of the mean differs from the standard deviation in that the standard error:

options.text: Measures the spread of individual scores in a sample
Measures the variability of sample means around the population mean
Is always larger than the standard deviation

why: The standard deviation describes the spread of individual scores within a sample. The standard error of the mean describes the variability of sample means around the population mean across repeated samples (SEM = σ/√ƛ). SEM decreases as sample size increases and is usually smaller than the SD.

optWhy.A: Spread of individual scores is the standard deviation, not the standard error.
optWhy.B: Correct. SE is the variability of sample means around the population mean.
optWhy.C: SE is usually smaller than SD (divided by √ƛ).
optWhy.D: SE decreases as sample size increases.

stem: The mean is affected by extreme values, whereas the median is not. This means the mean:

options.text: Is always the best measure of central tendency
Equals the mode in all distributions

why: Because the mean incorporates every score's value, extreme scores (outliers) pull it toward them. The median depends only on rank order and is robust to outliers. The mean is not always the best measure, is affected by skew, and does not always equal the mode.

optWhy.A: The mean is not always best; the median is preferable for skewed data.
optWhy.B: Correct. Extreme scores pull the mean, making it outlier-sensitive.
optWhy.C: The mean is affected by skew.
optWhy.D: Mean, median, and mode coincide only in symmetrical distributions.

stem: In a positively skewed distribution, the typical ordering of central tendency measures is:
why: In positive skew, the long tail of high values pulls the mean above the median, which is typically above the mode: Mean > Median > Mode. The reverse holds for negative skew.

optWhy.A: Mean < Median < Mode describes negative skew.
optWhy.B: Correct. Positive skew: Mean > Median > Mode.
optWhy.C: Equality holds only in symmetrical distributions.
optWhy.D: This ordering is not the standard positive-skew pattern.

stem: Sample variance divides by n–1 rather than n because:

options.text: It corrects for bias in estimating the population variance
It is required for calculating the mean
It always gives a whole number

why: Dividing by n–1 (Bessel's correction) makes the sample variance an unbiased estimator of the population variance. Dividing by n would underestimate the population variance on average.

optWhy.A: The purpose is unbiased estimation, not merely making it larger.
optWhy.B: Correct. n–1 corrects for bias in estimating the population variance.
optWhy.C: The mean does not require n–1.
optWhy.D: n–1 does not guarantee a whole number.

stem: Group A has SD = 5 and Group B has SD = 15 on the same measure. Group B:
why: A larger standard deviation indicates greater variability (spread) of scores around the mean. Group B's SD of 15 shows substantially greater variability than Group A's SD of 5. SD does not indicate the mean.

optWhy.A: A larger SD means greater, not less, variability.
optWhy.B: Correct. SD = 15 indicates greater variability than SD = 5.
optWhy.C: Different SDs mean different variability.
optWhy.D: SD is a measure of spread, not the mean.

stem: The sum of deviations of scores from their mean is:
why: By definition, the sum of deviations from the mean (Σ(X − X̄)) is always zero: positive and negative deviations cancel out. It is not the variance or SD.

optWhy.A: Positive and negative deviations cancel, so the sum is zero.
optWhy.B: Correct. Σ(X − X̄) = 0 by definition of the mean.
optWhy.C: The variance is the average squared deviation, not the sum of deviations.
optWhy.D: The SD is the square root of the variance.

stem: For ordinal data such as Likert-scale responses, the most appropriate measure of central tendency is:
why: Ordinal data have rank order but no equal intervals, so the mean is not strictly appropriate. The median (the middle rank) is the appropriate measure of central tendency for ordinal data. SD and variance are measures of dispersion, not central tendency.

optWhy.A: The mean assumes equal intervals, which ordinal data lack.
optWhy.B: Correct. The median is appropriate for ordinal data.
optWhy.C: SD is a measure of dispersion.
optWhy.D: Variance is a measure of dispersion.

stem: Test A: mean = 70, SD = 10. Test B: mean = 80, SD = 20. Which test shows greater relative variability?
why: Relative variability is compared via CV = SD/mean. Test A: CV = 10/70 ≈ 14.3%. Test B: CV = 20/80 = 25%. Test B has greater relative variability despite its higher mean, because its SD is proportionally larger.

optWhy.A: Test A's CV (14.3%) is lower than Test B's (25%).
optWhy.B: Correct. Test B's CV (25%) exceeds Test A's (14.3%).
optWhy.C: The CVs differ (14.3% vs 25%).
optWhy.D: Means and SDs are provided, so CV can be computed.

stem: A score X = 70 comes from a distribution with mean μ = 60 and SD σ = 10. The z-score is:

optWhy.B: 0.5 would result from a difference of 5.
optWhy.C: −1.0 would be for X = 50.
optWhy.D: 2.0 would be for X = 80.

stem: A distribution has μ = 50 and σ = 8. The raw score corresponding to z = 1.5 is:

optWhy.A: 58 corresponds to z = 1.0.
optWhy.B: Correct. 50 + 12 = 62.
optWhy.C: 65 corresponds to z = 1.875.
optWhy.D: 54 corresponds to z = 0.5.

stem: For a standard normal curve, the area between the mean and z = 1.0 is approximately:
why: From the standard normal table, the area between the mean (z = 0) and z = 1.0 is approximately 0.3413 (34.13%).

optWhy.A: Correct. Area between mean and z = 1.0 is 0.3413.
optWhy.B: 0.5000 is the area below the mean.
optWhy.C: 0.1587 is the area beyond z = 1.0.
optWhy.D: 0.8413 is the area below z = 1.0.

stem: A z-score of 1.0 corresponds to approximately which percentile rank?
why: A z-score of 1.0 has an area below it of approximately 0.8413, i.e., the 84th percentile.

optWhy.A: 50th percentile corresponds to z = 0.
optWhy.B: Correct. Area below z = 1.0 is 0.8413 ≈ 84th percentile.
optWhy.C: 16th percentile corresponds to z = −1.0.
optWhy.D: 95th percentile corresponds to z ≈ 1.645.

stem: Student A: X = 85, μ = 75, σ = 10. Student B: X = 90, μ = 80, σ = 15. Who performed better relative to their distribution?
why: z_A = (85−75)/10 = 1.0. z_B = (90−80)/15 = 0.67. Student A's z-score is higher, so A performed better relative to their distribution despite a lower raw score.

optWhy.A: Correct. z_A = 1.0 > z_B = 0.67.
optWhy.B: Student B's raw score is higher but relative performance is lower.
optWhy.C: The z-scores differ (1.0 vs 0.67).
optWhy.D: Means and SDs are provided, so z-scores can be computed.

stem: Group 1: n = 10, mean = 25, SD = 4. Group 2: n = 10, mean = 20, SD = 5. The independent-samples t-statistic is approximately:

optWhy.B: 1.50 underestimates the t-statistic.
optWhy.C: 3.00 overestimates the t-statistic.
optWhy.D: 5.00 is the raw mean difference, not t.

stem: Pre–post differences for 5 participants: 3, 5, 2, 4, 6. The paired-samples t-statistic is approximately:

optWhy.A: Correct. Mean diff = 4; SE ≈ 0.707; t ≈ 5.66.
optWhy.B: 4.00 is the mean difference, not t.
optWhy.C: 2.00 underestimates t.
optWhy.D: 1.00 underestimates t.

stem: For an independent-samples t-test with n1 = 10 and n2 = 10, the degrees of freedom are:

optWhy.A: Correct. df = 10 + 10 − 2 = 18.
optWhy.B: 9 is df for a single sample of 10.
optWhy.C: 19 is df for a paired test with n = 20 or total n−1.
optWhy.D: 20 is the total sample size.

stem: An independent-samples t-test yields t(18) = 2.47, p < .05. The correct interpretation is:

options.text: The null hypothesis is definitely true
Reject H₀; there is a statistically significant difference between groups

why: With df = 18 and p < .05, the result is statistically significant at the .05 level, so we reject H₀ and conclude there is a statistically significant difference between groups. This does not prove H₀ is false or that groups are identical.

optWhy.A: Rejecting H₀ means we do not conclude it is true.
optWhy.B: Correct. p < .05 leads to rejecting H₀ and concluding a significant difference.
optWhy.C: A significant result indicates the groups differ.
optWhy.D: We reject, not accept, H₀ when p < .05.

stem: Group 1 mean = 25, Group 2 mean = 20, pooled SD = 4. Cohen's d is:
why: Cohen's d = (M1 − M2)/SD_pooled = (25 − 20)/4 = 5/4 = 1.25, a large effect.

optWhy.A: Correct. 5/4 = 1.25.
optWhy.B: 0.80 is the conventional threshold for a large effect, not this value.
optWhy.C: 5.00 is the raw mean difference.
optWhy.D: 0.20 is the conventional threshold for a small effect.

stem: The normal probability curve is:
why: The normal curve is symmetrical, unimodal, bell-shaped, with mean = median = mode, and asymptotic tails. It is not skewed or bimodal.

optWhy.A: Correct. The normal curve is symmetrical and unimodal.
optWhy.B: The normal curve is not skewed.
optWhy.C: The normal curve has one mode (unimodal).
optWhy.D: The normal curve is not skewed.

stem: A leptokurtic distribution is:

options.text: More peaked than normal with heavier tails

why: Leptokurtic distributions are more peaked than normal with heavier (fatter) tails. Platykurtic are flatter; mesokurtic are normal. Kurtosis is about peakedness/tails, not skew.

optWhy.A: Flatter than normal is platykurtic.
optWhy.B: Correct. Leptokurtic = more peaked, heavier tails.
optWhy.C: Exactly normal is mesokurtic.
optWhy.D: Skew is a separate dimension from kurtosis.

stem: A z-score of −1.5 indicates a score:
why: A negative z-score indicates a score below the mean; −1.5 means 1.5 standard deviations below the mean.

optWhy.A: −1.5 is below, not above, the mean.
optWhy.B: Correct. −1.5 SD = 1.5 standard deviations below the mean.
optWhy.C: z = 0 equals the mean.
optWhy.D: A z-score is in SD units, not percentile points.

stem: Parametric tests assume:

options.text: Normality, homogeneity of variance, interval/ratio data, and independence

why: Parametric tests (e.g., t, ANOVA) assume normality of the sampling distribution/population, homogeneity of variance, interval or ratio level measurement, and independence of observations.

optWhy.A: Nominal data suit non-parametric tests like chi-square.
optWhy.B: Correct. These are the standard parametric assumptions.
optWhy.C: Parametric tests have specific assumptions.
optWhy.D: Ordinal data suit non-parametric tests.

stem: A researcher measures the same patients before and after therapy. The appropriate test is:
why: Measuring the same participants on two occasions creates related (paired) samples, so the paired-samples t-test is appropriate. Independent-samples t compares different groups; Mann–Whitney is non-parametric for independent groups; chi-square is for frequencies.

optWhy.A: Independent-samples t compares different groups, not the same people twice.
optWhy.B: Correct. Same participants measured twice = paired-samples t-test.
optWhy.C: Mann–Whitney is for independent groups and is non-parametric.
optWhy.D: Chi-square tests association in frequencies.

stem: A one-tailed test:

options.text: Tests for a difference in either direction
Tests for a difference in a specified direction

why: A one-tailed (directional) test places the entire α in one tail and tests for a difference in a specified direction. A two-tailed test splits α across both tails and is more conservative.

optWhy.A: Testing either direction is two-tailed.
optWhy.B: Correct. One-tailed tests a specified direction.
optWhy.C: One-tailed is less conservative (more power in one direction).
optWhy.D: One-tailed tests can be used with t-tests.

options.text: Reject H₀; the result is significant

why: Since p = .048 < α = .05, the result is statistically significant, so we reject H₀. We do not accept H₀, and the result is determinable.

optWhy.A: p < .05 means reject H₀, not fail to reject.
optWhy.B: Correct. p = .048 < .05, so reject H₀; result is significant.
optWhy.C: We never ‘accept’ H₀; we reject or fail to reject.
optWhy.D: p and α are given, so the decision is determinable.

stem: A researcher uses an independent-samples t-test, but the two groups have very different variances and the data are skewed. The main problem is:

options.text: Violation of parametric assumptions (normality, homogeneity of variance)

why: The independent-samples t-test assumes normality and homogeneity of variance. Skewed data and very different variances violate these assumptions, so the t-test is inappropriate (a non-parametric alternative such as Mann–Whitney U should be considered).

optWhy.A: Correct. Skewed data and unequal variances violate parametric assumptions.
optWhy.B: A large sample is not a problem.
optWhy.C: A continuous dependent variable is appropriate for a t-test.
optWhy.D: The t-test is parametric, not non-parametric.

stem: Data are ordinal, two independent groups, and distributions are skewed. The appropriate test is:
why: Ordinal data with skewed distributions and independent groups violate parametric assumptions; the Mann–Whitney U test (a non-parametric test for two independent samples) is appropriate. Independent-samples t and paired-samples t are parametric; Pearson r is for correlation.

optWhy.A: Independent-samples t requires interval/ratio data and normality.
optWhy.B: Correct. Mann–Whitney U suits ordinal, skewed, independent-group data.
optWhy.C: Paired-samples t is for related samples and is parametric.
optWhy.D: Pearson r measures correlation, not group differences.

stem: The standard error of the mean decreases as:
why: SEM = σ/√n, so SEM decreases as sample size n increases (and as SD decreases). It is not constant.

optWhy.A: Decreasing sample size increases SEM.
optWhy.B: Correct. SEM = σ/√n decreases as n increases.
optWhy.C: SEM depends on both SD and n.
optWhy.D: SEM changes with n and SD.

stem: p < .05 indicates:

options.text: The null hypothesis is definitely false
The result is statistically significant at the .05 level

why: p < .05 means the result is statistically significant at the .05 level (evidence against H₀). It does not prove H₀ false, indicate effect size, or guarantee replication.

optWhy.A: p < .05 does not prove H₀ definitely false.
optWhy.B: Correct. p < .05 = statistically significant at .05.
optWhy.C: Effect size is separate from p.
optWhy.D: Replication is not guaranteed by one p-value.

stem: Before choosing a parametric test, a researcher should:

options.text: Assess assumptions (normality, homogeneity, independence, level of measurement)
Use the most powerful test regardless

why: Parametric tests require checking assumptions: normality, homogeneity of variance, independence, and appropriate level of measurement. Assuming normality automatically or ignoring the design risks invalid conclusions.

optWhy.A: Normality must be assessed, not assumed.
optWhy.B: Correct. Assess all relevant assumptions before choosing a parametric test.
optWhy.C: Power is irrelevant if assumptions are violated.
optWhy.D: The research design determines the appropriate test.

stem: The central limit theorem states that:

options.text: The sampling distribution of the mean approaches normality as n increases

why: The central limit theorem states that the sampling distribution of the mean approaches a normal distribution as sample size increases, regardless of the population shape (with finite variance). It does not say all distributions are normal.

optWhy.A: Not all distributions are normal.
optWhy.B: Correct. The sampling distribution of the mean approaches normality as n increases.
optWhy.C: The population need not be normal.
optWhy.D: The median is not always normal.

stem: A z-test is used instead of a t-test when:
why: A z-test is used when the population standard deviation σ is known. A t-test is used when σ is unknown and estimated from the sample.

optWhy.A: Correct. Known population SD αs a z-test.
optWhy.B: A tiny sample typically calls for a t-test.
optWhy.C: Nominal data suit chi-square, not z or t.
optWhy.D: Skewed distributions violate parametric assumptions for both.

stem: A study finds p = .04 and Cohen's d = 0.10. The best conclusion is:
why: p = .04 < .05, so the result is statistically significant, but Cohen's d = 0.10 is a trivial effect (below the 0.2 small threshold). Statistical significance does not imply practical importance.

optWhy.A: Correct. Significant (p < .05) but trivial effect (d = 0.10).
optWhy.B: p = .04 < .05, so it is statistically significant.
optWhy.C: d = 0.10 is trivial, not large.
optWhy.D: One significant result is not conclusive proof.

optWhy.B: 3.00 is the mean difference, not t.

optWhy.A: 0 is too low.
optWhy.B: Correct. U = 1.
optWhy.C: 8 is U for group B; U is the smaller value.
optWhy.D: 9 is n1×n2, not U.

stem: Differences: +3, −1, +2, −4, +5. The Wilcoxon signed-rank statistic W is:
why: Absolute values: 3,1,2,4,5 → ranks 3,1,2,4,5. Signed ranks: +3, −1, +2, −4, +5. Sum of positive ranks = 3+2+5 = 10. Sum of negative ranks = 1+4 = 5. W = smaller sum = 5.

optWhy.A: 10 is the sum of positive ranks, not W (the smaller sum).
optWhy.B: 15 is the total of ranks.
optWhy.C: Correct. W = 5 (smaller of 10 and 5).
optWhy.D: 0 is incorrect.

optWhy.A: Correct. H ≈ 3.58.
optWhy.B: 4.50 overestimates H.
optWhy.C: 5.50 overestimates H.
optWhy.D: 6.50 overestimates H.

optWhy.A: Correct. χ²_F = 0.5.
optWhy.B: 1.0 overestimates.
optWhy.C: 2.0 overestimates.
optWhy.D: 0.0 is incorrect.

stem: Group 1 mean = 25, Group 2 mean = 20, pooled SD = 5. Cohen's d is:
why: Cohen's d = (M1 − M2)/SD_pooled = (25 − 20)/5 = 5/5 = 1.0, a large effect.

optWhy.A: Correct. 5/5 = 1.0.
optWhy.B: 0.5 is the conventional threshold for a medium effect.
optWhy.C: 2.0 would require a mean difference of 10.
optWhy.D: 5.0 is the raw mean difference.

stem: Group 1 mean = 30, Group 2 mean = 24, SD = 3. Cohen's d is:
why: Cohen's d = (M1 − M2)/SD = (30 − 24)/3 = 6/3 = 2.0, a very large effect.

optWhy.A: 1.0 would require a mean difference of 3.
optWhy.B: 1.5 would require a mean difference of 4.5.
optWhy.C: Correct. 6/3 = 2.0.
optWhy.D: 3.0 would require a mean difference of 9.

sub: Type I and Type II errors
stem: If β = 0.20, the statistical power is:

optWhy.A: 0.20 is β, not power.
optWhy.B: Correct. Power = 1 − 0.20 = 0.80.
optWhy.C: 0.05 is the conventional α.
optWhy.D: 0.90 would require β = 0.10.

why: r² = 0.30×0.30 = 0.09 (9% shared variance).

optWhy.A: 0.30 is r, not r².
optWhy.B: Correct. r² = 0.09.
optWhy.C: 0.90 is incorrect.
optWhy.D: 0.03 is incorrect.

stem: If r = 0.50, r² is:
why: r² = 0.50×0.50 = 0.25 (25% shared variance).

optWhy.A: Correct. r² = 0.25.
optWhy.B: 0.50 is r, not r².
optWhy.C: 0.75 is incorrect.
optWhy.D: 0.05 is incorrect.

optWhy.B: Correct. √26 ≈ 5.10.
optWhy.C: 5.20 overestimates.
optWhy.D: 6.00 is SD2, not the pooled SD.

stem: Non-parametric tests are valued because they:

options.text: Always have more power than parametric tests
Make fewer assumptions about the population distribution (e.g., normality not required)

why: Non-parametric tests make fewer or weaker assumptions (often no normality assumption) and can be used with ordinal data or small samples. They do not always have more power than parametric tests when parametric assumptions hold.

optWhy.A: Parametric tests are generally more powerful when their assumptions are met.
optWhy.B: Correct. Fewer distributional assumptions is the key advantage.
optWhy.C: Non-parametric tests often use ordinal or ranked data.
optWhy.D: They are useful for small samples too.

stem: The sign test is appropriate for:

options.text: Comparing means of two independent groups
The direction of change in paired (before–after) data

why: The sign test uses only the direction (sign) of change in paired data (e.g., improvement vs. decline), ignoring magnitude. It is a simple non-parametric test for related samples.

optWhy.A: Comparing means of independent groups uses t or Mann–Whitney.
optWhy.B: Correct. The sign test uses direction of change in paired data.
optWhy.C: Correlation is not tested by the sign test.
optWhy.D: One-way ANOVA compares k independent group means.

stem: Match the test (List-I) to its design (List-II).
why: Mann–Whitney U compares two independent groups; Wilcoxon signed-rank compares two related/paired groups.

optWhy.A: Correct. A-1 (independent), B-2 (related/paired).
optWhy.B: Reverses the designs.
optWhy.C: B-1 is wrong; Wilcoxon is not for independent groups.
optWhy.D: A-2 is wrong; Mann–Whitney is not for related groups.

stem: Read Assertion (A) and Reason (R), then choose the correct option.
assertion: Kruskal–Wallis H is the non-parametric alternative to one-way ANOVA for independent groups.
reason: It compares rank sums across k independent groups without requiring normality.

options.text: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion
Assertion is true but Reason is false
Assertion is false but Reason is true

why: Kruskal–Wallis H extends the Mann–Whitney U to k independent groups, using rank sums rather than raw means, and does not require normality. Both statements are true, and the reason explains the assertion.

optWhy.A: Correct. Both are true and the reason explains the assertion.
optWhy.B: The reason does explain the assertion.
optWhy.C: The reason is true.
optWhy.D: The assertion is true.

stem: Which statements about Friedman test and repeated-measures ANOVA are correct?
statements: 1. The Friedman test is the non-parametric equivalent of repeated-measures ANOVA.
2. The Friedman test requires normality of the population.
3. The Friedman test uses ranks within each block (participant).
4. Repeated-measures ANOVA is parametric and assumes sphericity.
why: Statement 1 is correct: Friedman is the non-parametric counterpart to repeated-measures ANOVA. Statement 2 is incorrect: Friedman does not require normality. Statement 3 is correct: it ranks within each block. Statement 4 is correct: repeated-measures ANOVA is parametric and assumes sphericity.

optWhy.A: Omits statements 3 and 4, which are correct.
optWhy.B: Correct. Statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct; statement 2 is incorrect.
optWhy.C: Statement 2 is incorrect.
optWhy.D: Statement 2 is incorrect.

stem: Data are ordinal, two independent groups, and distributions are skewed. The appropriate test is:
why: Ordinal data with skewed distributions and independent groups violate parametric assumptions; the Mann–Whitney U test (non-parametric, two independent samples) is appropriate.

optWhy.A: Independent-samples t requires interval/ratio data and normality.
optWhy.B: Correct. Mann–Whitney U suits ordinal, skewed, independent-group data.
optWhy.C: Paired-samples t is for related samples and is parametric.
optWhy.D: Pearson r measures correlation, not group differences.

stem: Statistical power is:

options.text: The probability of a Type I error
The probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis (1 − β)
The probability of a Type II error

why: Power = 1 − β, the probability of correctly rejecting H₀ when it is false (detecting a true effect). It is not the Type I error (α), Type II error (β), or effect size.

optWhy.A: Type I error is α.
optWhy.B: Correct. Power = 1 − β.
optWhy.C: Type II error is β.
optWhy.D: Effect size is a separate concept.

sub: Type I vs Type II errors
stem: Type I error and Type II error differ in that Type I error:

options.text: Is failing to reject a false null hypothesis
Is rejecting a true null hypothesis (α)

why: Type I error = rejecting a true null hypothesis (probability α). Type II error = failing to reject a false null hypothesis (probability β). Power = 1 − β.

optWhy.A: Failing to reject a false null is Type II error.
optWhy.B: Correct. Type I error = rejecting a true null (α).
optWhy.C: Power is 1 − β, not Type I error.
optWhy.D: β denotes Type II error.

key: Type I vs Type II error

stem: Which statements about effect-size interpretation are correct?
statements: 1. Cohen's d = 0.2 is conventionally a small effect.
2. Cohen's d = 0.8 is conventionally a large effect.
3. r = 0.1 is conventionally a small effect for correlation.
4. A larger effect size always means a smaller p-value.
why: Statement 1 is correct (d = 0.2 small). Statement 2 is correct (d = 0.8 large). Statement 3 is correct (r = 0.1 small). Statement 4 is incorrect: p-value depends on both effect size and sample size, so a large effect with a tiny sample may not be significant.

optWhy.A: Omits statement 3, which is correct.
optWhy.B: Correct. Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct; statement 4 is incorrect.
optWhy.C: Statement 4 is incorrect.
optWhy.D: Statement 4 is incorrect.

stem: A study finds p = .04 and Cohen's d = 0.10. The best conclusion is:
why: p = .04 < .05, so the result is statistically significant, but Cohen's d = 0.10 is a trivial effect (below the 0.2 small threshold). Statistical significance does not imply practical importance.

optWhy.A: Correct. Significant (p < .05) but trivial effect (d = 0.10).
optWhy.B: p = .04 < .05, so it is statistically significant.
optWhy.C: d = 0.10 is trivial, not large.
optWhy.D: One significant result is not conclusive proof.

sub: A priori vs post hoc power
stem: A priori power analysis is conducted:

options.text: After data collection to interpret results
Before data collection to plan sample size

why: A priori power analysis is done before the study to determine the sample size needed for a desired power. Post hoc power is calculated after the study and is controversial.

optWhy.A: After data collection is post hoc power.
optWhy.B: Correct. A priori power plans sample size before the study.
optWhy.C: A priori power applies to parametric and non-parametric tests.
optWhy.D: Effect size is an input to, not a replacement for, power analysis.

key: A priori vs post hoc power

stem: Which of the following would increase statistical power?

options.text: Increasing the effect size or sample size
Using a more stringent alpha (e.g., .001) only

why: Power increases with larger effect size, larger sample size, larger alpha, and lower variability. Decreasing sample size, using a more stringent alpha, or increasing variability reduces power.

optWhy.A: Decreasing sample size reduces power.
optWhy.B: Correct. Larger effect size or sample size increases power.
optWhy.C: A more stringent alpha (.001) reduces power.
optWhy.D: Increasing variability reduces power.

stem: A researcher compares anxiety across three independent clinics using ordinal ratings, with skewed distributions and unequal clinic sizes. The appropriate analysis is:
why: Three independent groups, ordinal data, skewed distributions, and unequal sizes violate one-way ANOVA assumptions (normality, homogeneity, interval data). The Kruskal–Wallis H test is the non-parametric alternative for k independent groups.

optWhy.A: One-way ANOVA requires interval/ratio data, normality, and homogeneity of variance.
optWhy.B: Correct. Kruskal–Wallis H suits ordinal, skewed, independent k-group data.
optWhy.C: Paired-samples t is for two related groups.
optWhy.D: Pearson r measures correlation.

stem: For X = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] and Y = [2, 4, 5, 4, 6], the Pearson correlation r is approximately:

optWhy.A: 0.50 underestimates r.
optWhy.B: Correct. r≈0.85.
optWhy.C: 0.30 underestimates r.
optWhy.D: 1.00 would require a perfect linear relation.

stem: Ranks: X = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], Y = [2, 1, 4, 5, 3]. The Spearman ρ is:

optWhy.A: -0.60 is the wrong sign.
optWhy.B: 0.00 would indicate no monotonic relation.
optWhy.C: Correct. ρ = 0.60.
optWhy.D: 1.00 would require perfect rank agreement.

stem: For X = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10] and Y = [5, 3, 7, 1, 9], the Pearson correlation r is:

optWhy.A: 0.90 overestimates r.
optWhy.B: 0.70 overestimates r.
optWhy.C: Correct. r = 0.30.
optWhy.D: 0.50 overestimates r.

stem: Given r(XY)=0.60, r(XZ)=0.50, r(YZ)=0.40, the partial correlation r(XY.Z) is approximately:

optWhy.A: Correct. r(XY.Z)≈0.50.
optWhy.B: 0.60 is the zero-order r(XY).
optWhy.C: 0.40 is r(YZ).
optWhy.D: 0.30 underestimates the partial correlation.

stem: If r = 0.70, the coefficient of determination r² is:
why: r² = 0.70×0.70 = 0.49 (49% shared variance).

optWhy.A: 0.70 is r, not r².
optWhy.B: 0.14 is incorrect.
optWhy.C: Correct. r² = 0.49.
optWhy.D: 0.30 is incorrect.

stem: If r = 0.60, r² is:
why: r² = 0.60×0.60 = 0.36 (36% shared variance).

optWhy.A: 0.60 is r, not r².
optWhy.B: Correct. r² = 0.36.
optWhy.C: 0.64 is incorrect.
optWhy.D: 0.16 is incorrect.

stem: For X = [1, 2, 3] and Y = [2, 4, 6], the Pearson correlation r is:
why: Y increases perfectly linearly with X (Y = 2X), so r = 1.00.

optWhy.A: -1.00 would be perfect negative.
optWhy.B: 0.00 would be no linear relation.
optWhy.C: 0.50 underestimates.
optWhy.D: Correct. Perfect positive linear relation, r = 1.00.

stem: If r = -0.50, the coefficient of determination r² is:
why: r² = (-0.50)×(-0.50) = 0.25. r² is always non-negative; the negative sign of r indicates direction only.

optWhy.A: 0.50 is |r|, not r².
optWhy.B: Correct. r² = 0.25.
optWhy.C: r² cannot be negative.
optWhy.D: 0.05 is incorrect.

stem: A significant correlation between ice-cream sales and drowning incidents does not imply causation because:

options.text: Both are caused by a third variable (hot weather)

why: A correlation between two variables may reflect a third variable influencing both (a common-cause or confounding explanation), rather than one causing the other. Correlation alone cannot establish causation.

optWhy.A: Correct. A third variable (temperature) explains the association.
optWhy.B: Ice-cream does not cause drowning.
optWhy.C: Correlation does not imply causation.
optWhy.D: Sample size does not resolve the causation issue.

stem: Pearson r is appropriate when:

options.text: Both variables are interval/ratio and linearly related

why: Pearson r assumes interval/ratio data, linearity, and approximately normal distributions. It measures linear association. For ordinal or non-linear/monotonic data, Spearman is more appropriate.

optWhy.A: Ordinal data suit Spearman, not Pearson.
optWhy.B: Correct. Pearson r suits interval/ratio, linearly related variables.
optWhy.C: Nominal data are not suitable for Pearson r.
optWhy.D: Pearson r measures linear, not non-linear, association.

stem: Restriction of range (e.g., selecting only high-scoring applicants) typically:

options.text: Has no effect on the correlation

why: Restricting the range of one or both variables reduces variability and therefore reduces the observed correlation, potentially masking a true relationship.

optWhy.A: Restriction of range reduces, not increases, the observed correlation.
optWhy.B: Correct. Less variability yields a smaller correlation.
optWhy.C: Restriction of range affects the correlation.
optWhy.D: It affects variability and correlation, not only the mean.

sub: Outliers and their effects on correlation
stem: An outlier in a correlation analysis:

options.text: Can strongly inflate or deflate the correlation

why: Outliers (especially influential points) can strongly distort Pearson r, either inflating or deflating it depending on their position relative to the trend. Correlations should be examined with scatterplots to detect outliers.

optWhy.A: Outliers can substantially affect correlation.
optWhy.B: Correct. Outliers can inflate or deflate r.
optWhy.C: Outliers do not always increase r.
optWhy.D: Outliers affect correlation and regression, not only the mean.

stem: A zero Pearson correlation means:

options.text: There is no linear relationship (a non-linear one may exist)

why: Pearson r measures linear association. r = 0 means no linear relationship, but a non-linear (e.g., curvilinear) relationship may still exist. It does not imply complete unrelatedness or causation.

optWhy.A: A non-linear relationship may still exist.
optWhy.B: Correct. r = 0 means no linear relationship.
optWhy.C: Zero correlation does not imply causation.
optWhy.D: Zero correlation does not imply zero variance.

stem: Partial correlation:

options.text: Measures the relationship between two variables controlling for a third
Is always larger than zero-order correlation
Is the same as multiple correlation

why: Partial correlation measures the association between two variables after removing the effect of one or more other variables. It is not always larger than zero-order correlation, requires at least three variables, and differs from multiple correlation.

optWhy.A: Correct. Partial correlation controls for a third variable.
optWhy.B: Partial correlation can be smaller or larger than zero-order.
optWhy.C: Partial correlation requires at least three variables.
optWhy.D: Multiple correlation involves one dependent variable and multiple predictors.

stem: Multiple correlation (R):

options.text: Measures the relationship between one dependent variable and a set of predictors
Is the same as simple correlation

why: Multiple correlation R measures the association between a single dependent variable and a set of two or more predictor variables collectively. It is non-negative and requires multiple predictors.

optWhy.A: Correct. R relates one DV to multiple predictors.
optWhy.B: Multiple R is non-negative.
optWhy.C: Multiple correlation requires multiple predictors.
optWhy.D: Simple correlation involves two variables; multiple involves more.

stem: Point-biserial correlation is used when:

options.text: One variable is a true dichotomy and the other is continuous
One variable is nominal with three categories

why: Point-biserial correlation is used when one variable is a true dichotomous variable (e.g., gender, pass/fail) and the other is continuous. It is mathematically equivalent to Pearson r applied to a dichotomous and a continuous variable.

optWhy.A: Two continuous variables use Pearson r.
optWhy.B: Correct. Point-biserial = true dichotomy + continuous.
optWhy.C: Ordinal variables use Spearman.
optWhy.D: Nominal with 3+ categories is not point-biserial.

stem: Match the special correlation (List-I) to its appropriate data situation (List-II).
listII: B. Underlying continuous variable and a dichotomised continuous variable
why: Point-biserial: true dichotomy + continuous (A-1). Biserial: underlying continuous dichotomy + continuous (B-2). Tetrachoric: two underlying continuous dichotomies (C-3). Phi: two true dichotomies (D-4).

optWhy.A: Correct. A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4.
optWhy.B: A-2 is wrong; point-biserial is not underlying-dichotomy + continuous.
optWhy.C: B-3 is wrong; biserial is not two underlying dichotomies.
optWhy.D: A-4 is wrong; point-biserial is not two true dichotomies.

stem: A researcher correlates gender (male/female) with scores on a continuous anxiety test. The appropriate coefficient is:
why: Gender is a true dichotomy and anxiety score is continuous, so the point-biserial correlation is appropriate. Tetrachoric assumes two underlying continuous dichotomies; phi requires two true dichotomies.

optWhy.A: Pearson r is mathematically equivalent here but point-biserial is the named choice for dichotomy + continuous.
optWhy.B: Correct. Gender (dichotomy) + anxiety (continuous) = point-biserial.
optWhy.C: Tetrachoric assumes two underlying continuous dichotomies.
optWhy.D: Phi requires two true dichotomies.

stem: A correlation matrix:
why: A correlation matrix displays the pairwise correlation coefficients among a set of variables, allowing inspection of all bivariate relationships at once. It does not prove causation and contains both positive and negative values.

optWhy.A: Correct. A correlation matrix shows pairwise correlations among multiple variables.
optWhy.B: A matrix contains many correlations, not one.
optWhy.C: A matrix contains positive and negative correlations.
optWhy.D: A correlation matrix does not prove causation.

stem: Read Assertion (A) and Reason (R), then choose the correct option.
assertion: Biserial correlation is used when a continuous variable has been artificially dichotomised.
reason: It assumes the underlying dichotomous variable is continuous and normally distributed.

options.text: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion
Assertion is true but Reason is false
Assertion is false but Reason is true

why: Biserial correlation is used when one variable is continuous and the other is a dichotomisation of an underlying continuous variable (e.g., test score vs. pass/fail derived from the score). It assumes normality of the underlying continuous variable. Both statements are true, and the reason explains the assertion.

optWhy.A: Correct. Both are true and the reason explains the assertion.
optWhy.B: The reason does explain the assertion.
optWhy.C: The reason is true.
optWhy.D: The assertion is true.

stem: The phi coefficient is used when:
why: The phi coefficient is a measure of association for two true dichotomous variables (e.g., gender by pass/fail) in a 2×2 contingency table. It is mathematically equivalent to Pearson r for two dichotomies.

optWhy.A: Two continuous variables use Pearson r.
optWhy.B: Correct. Phi = two true dichotomies.
optWhy.C: One continuous variable uses point-biserial with a dichotomy.
optWhy.D: Ordinal variables use Spearman.

stem: A study finds r = 0.40 between study time and exam scores (p < .05). The appropriate interpretation is:

options.text: Study time causes higher exam scores
There is a moderate positive association; causation cannot be inferred

why: r = 0.40 indicates a moderate positive linear association, and p < .05 indicates it is statistically significant. However, correlation does not establish causation; a third variable may explain the association.

optWhy.A: Correlation does not establish causation.
optWhy.B: Correct. Moderate positive association; no causal inference.
optWhy.C: r = 0.40 is moderate, not perfect (1.00).
optWhy.D: The result is statistically significant and meaningful.

stem: Which statements about special correlation coefficients are correct?
statements: 1. Phi is used for two true dichotomies.
2. Point-biserial is used for a true dichotomy and a continuous variable.
3. Tetrachoric is used for two underlying continuous dichotomies.
4. Biserial and point-biserial are identical.
why: Statement 1 is correct (phi = two true dichotomies). Statement 2 is correct (point-biserial = true dichotomy + continuous). Statement 3 is correct (tetrachoric = two underlying continuous dichotomies). Statement 4 is incorrect: biserial assumes an underlying continuous dichotomy, whereas point-biserial uses a true dichotomy.

optWhy.A: Omits statement 3, which is correct.
optWhy.B: Correct. Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct; statement 4 is incorrect.
optWhy.C: Statement 4 is incorrect.
optWhy.D: Statement 4 is incorrect.

stem: A study finds p = .03 and r = 0.10 between a new drug and symptom reduction. The best conclusion is:

options.text: Statistically significant but a very small/practically trivial association

why: p = .03 < .05, so the association is statistically significant, but r = 0.10 (r² = 0.01, 1% shared variance) is a very small/practically trivial effect. Statistical significance does not imply practical importance or causation.

optWhy.A: r = 0.10 is a very small effect, not strong.
optWhy.B: Correct. Significant but practically trivial (r² = 0.01).
optWhy.C: Correlation does not establish causation.
optWhy.D: p = .03 < .05, so it is statistically significant.

stem: A zero Pearson correlation between two variables means:

options.text: There is no linear relationship (a non-linear relationship may exist)

why: Pearson r detects only linear association. r = 0 means no linear relationship, but the variables may be related non-linearly (e.g., curvilinearly). It does not imply complete unrelatedness or causation.

optWhy.A: A non-linear relationship may still exist.
optWhy.B: Correct. r = 0 means no linear relationship.
optWhy.C: Zero correlation does not imply causation.
optWhy.D: Zero correlation does not imply zero variance.

stem: Regression equation Y = 5 + 2X. For X = 10, the predicted Y is:

optWhy.A: 20 is bX only, omitting the intercept.
optWhy.C: 30 overestimates.
optWhy.D: 15 is a + X, not a + bX.

stem: Given r = 0.8, SDy = 10, SDx = 5, the regression slope b is:

optWhy.A: Correct. b = 1.6.
optWhy.B: 0.8 is r, not the slope.
optWhy.C: 2.0 is SDy/SDx only, omitting r.
optWhy.D: 0.4 is r x (SDx/SDy), the inverse.

stem: Regression line: mean Y = 50, mean X = 20, slope b = 2. The intercept a is:

optWhy.A: 50 is mean Y, not the intercept.
optWhy.B: 40 is b mean X, not the intercept.
optWhy.C: Correct. 50 - 40 = 10.
optWhy.D: 20 is mean X.

stem: Regression: Y = 10 + 2X. For X = 15, observed Y = 45. The residual is:

optWhy.A: Correct. Residual = 45 - 40 = 5.
optWhy.B: 40 is the predicted value, not the residual.
optWhy.C: 45 is the observed value.
optWhy.D: -5 is Y - Y, the reverse.

stem: Multiple regression: Y = 10 + 2X1 + 3X2. For X1 = 5, X2 = 4, the predicted Y is:

optWhy.A: 30 omits one term.
optWhy.C: 34 overestimates.
optWhy.D: 28 underestimates.

stem: If R = 0.64, the proportion of variance explained is:
why: R = 0.64 means 64% of the variance in the dependent variable is explained by the regression model.

optWhy.A: Correct. R = 0.64 (64% explained variance).
optWhy.B: 0.80 is R (the square root), not R.
optWhy.C: 0.36 is the unexplained variance (1 - 0.64).
optWhy.D: 0.50 is incorrect.

stem: Regression assumes:

options.text: Linearity, homoscedasticity, independence of errors, and normality of residuals

why: Linear regression assumes linearity (straight-line relationship), homoscedasticity (constant error variance), independence of errors, and normality of residuals. Violations bias inference.

optWhy.A: Correct. These are the core regression assumptions.
optWhy.B: Linearity is necessary but not sufficient.
optWhy.C: Regression uses quantitative predictors; categorical predictors need coding.
optWhy.D: Regression has specific assumptions.

stem: Standardised regression coefficients (beta) differ from unstandardised coefficients (b) in that beta:

options.text: Depends on the units of measurement
Is expressed in standard deviation units and is unit-free

why: Unstandardised b depends on the original units of X and Y. Standardised beta is expressed in SD units and is unit-free, allowing comparison of predictor importance across variables measured on different scales.

optWhy.A: Unstandardised b depends on units; beta does not.
optWhy.B: Correct. beta is unit-free (SD units) and comparable across predictors.
optWhy.C: beta is not always larger than b.
optWhy.D: beta is designed to be compared across predictors.

stem: Multicollinearity refers to:

options.text: High correlation between X and Y

why: Multicollinearity occurs when two or more predictor variables are highly correlated with each other, inflating standard errors and making individual coefficients unstable. It is distinct from X-Y correlation, non-normal residuals, and heteroscedasticity.

optWhy.A: Correct. Multicollinearity = high intercorrelations among predictors.
optWhy.B: High X-Y correlation is desirable (strong prediction), not multicollinearity.
optWhy.C: Non-normal residuals are a separate assumption violation.
optWhy.D: Heteroscedasticity is non-constant error variance.

stem: Regression can predict an outcome, but:

options.text: Prediction does not imply causation without a causal design
It only works with experimental data

why: Regression predicts Y from X, but prediction does not imply causation. Causal claims require an appropriate research design (e.g., random assignment) and control of confounds. Observational regression associations may reflect third variables.

optWhy.A: Regression does not automatically establish causation.
optWhy.B: Correct. Prediction is distinct from causal explanation.
optWhy.C: Regression is useful for prediction even without causation.
optWhy.D: Regression works with observational as well as experimental data.

stem: Adjusted R differs from R in that it:

options.text: Penalises the addition of unnecessary predictors

why: Adjusted R adjusts R for the number of predictors relative to sample size, penalising the addition of predictors that do not improve the model. It is never larger than R and can be negative.

optWhy.A: Correct. Adjusted R penalises unnecessary predictors.
optWhy.B: Adjusted R is never larger than R.
optWhy.C: Adjusted R explicitly accounts for the number of predictors.
optWhy.D: Adjusted R cannot exceed 1.

stem: A partial regression coefficient in multiple regression represents:

options.text: The unique effect of one predictor controlling for the others
The total correlation between X and Y
The effect of all predictors combined

why: A partial regression coefficient shows the expected change in Y for a one-unit change in that predictor, holding all other predictors constant (unique effect). It is distinct from zero-order correlation and multicollinearity.

optWhy.A: Correct. Partial coefficient = unique effect controlling for other predictors.
optWhy.B: Zero-order correlation is the bivariate X-Y relationship.
optWhy.C: All predictors combined is represented by the model/R, not one coefficient.
optWhy.D: Correlation among predictors is multicollinearity, not a coefficient.

stem: Factor analysis is primarily used to:

options.text: Identify underlying factors (dimensions) that explain patterns of correlations

why: Factor analysis identifies latent underlying factors (dimensions) that explain the correlations among a set of observed variables. It is not for group differences, prediction, or causation.

optWhy.A: Correct. Factor analysis identifies underlying latent factors.
optWhy.B: Group differences are tested by ANOVA/t-tests.
optWhy.C: Prediction is regression.
optWhy.D: Factor analysis does not establish causation.

stem: Match the method (List-I) to what it analyses (List-II).
why: EFA analyses common (shared) variance to uncover latent factors; PCA analyses total variance (including unique and error variance) to reduce data.

optWhy.A: Correct. A-1 (common variance), B-2 (total variance).
optWhy.B: Reverses the methods.
optWhy.C: PCA does not analyse only common variance.
optWhy.D: EFA does not analyse only total variance.

stem: KMO = 0.72 and Bartlett's test is significant (p < .05). This indicates:

options.text: Data are suitable for factor analysis
Data are unsuitable for factor analysis
The correlation matrix is an identity matrix

why: KMO > 0.60 indicates adequate sampling for factor analysis (0.72 is acceptable). A significant Bartlett's test indicates the correlation matrix is not an identity matrix (correlations exist), supporting factor analysis.

optWhy.A: Correct. KMO 0.72 is adequate; significant Bartlett's means correlations exist.
optWhy.B: Data are suitable, not unsuitable.
optWhy.C: A significant Bartlett's means the matrix is NOT an identity matrix.
optWhy.D: KMO and Bartlett's address suitability, not sample size directly.

stem: In factor retention, the Kaiser criterion retains factors with:
why: The Kaiser criterion retains factors with eigenvalues greater than 1 (a factor explains more variance than a single original variable). The scree plot is a complementary graphical method.

optWhy.A: Correct. Retain factors with eigenvalue > 1.
optWhy.B: Eigenvalue < 1 means the factor explains less than one variable.
optWhy.C: Eigenvalue 0 means no variance explained.
optWhy.D: Negative eigenvalues indicate problems (e.g., small sample), not retention.

stem: A factor loading represents:

options.text: The correlation between an observed variable and a factor

why: A factor loading is the correlation between an observed variable and a (latent) factor; the squared loading is the proportion of that variable's variance explained by the factor. Communality is the total variance of a variable explained by all factors.

optWhy.A: Correct. A factor loading = variable-factor correlation.
optWhy.B: Factor correlations are in a factor correlation matrix (oblique rotation).
optWhy.C: Squared loadings give variance explained; communalities sum them.
optWhy.D: The number of factors is a retention decision, not a loading.

stem: Match the rotation (List-I) to its assumption (List-II).
why: Orthogonal rotation (varimax) keeps factors uncorrelated (90 degrees axes). Oblique rotation (promax) allows factors to correlate, which is often more realistic for psychological constructs.

optWhy.A: Correct. A-1 (orthogonal = uncorrelated), B-2 (oblique = correlated).
optWhy.B: Reverses the assumptions.
optWhy.C: Oblique allows correlated factors.
optWhy.D: Orthogonal does not allow correlated factors.

stem: Communality represents:

options.text: The proportion of a variable's variance explained by all retained factors

why: Communality (h) is the proportion of a given variable's variance that is explained by the retained factors collectively. It differs from a factor loading (one variable-factor correlation) and an eigenvalue (variance explained by one factor).

optWhy.A: Correct. Communality = variance of a variable explained by all factors.
optWhy.B: Factor correlations are in a factor correlation matrix.
optWhy.C: Number of factors is a retention decision.
optWhy.D: Eigenvalue is variance explained by one factor.

stem: A researcher wants to uncover latent psychological constructs underlying a questionnaire. The appropriate method is:
why: EFA uncovers latent constructs (factors) underlying observed variables, modelling common variance. PCA reduces data using total variance and is not designed to uncover latent constructs. Regression predicts; ANOVA compares means.

optWhy.A: PCA reduces data using total variance, not latent constructs.
optWhy.B: Correct. EFA uncovers latent psychological constructs.
optWhy.C: Regression predicts an outcome.
optWhy.D: ANOVA compares group means.

stem: Factor extraction methods include:

options.text: Principal axis factoring and maximum likelihood

why: Extraction methods (how factors are derived) include principal axis factoring and maximum likelihood. Varimax/promax are rotations; Kaiser/scree are retention criteria; KMO/Bartlett's assess suitability.

optWhy.A: Correct. PAF and ML are extraction methods.
optWhy.B: Varimax/promax are rotation methods.
optWhy.C: Kaiser/scree are retention criteria.
optWhy.D: KMO/Bartlett's assess factorability.

stem: A low communality for a variable indicates:

options.text: The factors explain little of that variable's variance
The variable has a high factor loading on all factors

why: A low communality means the retained factors explain little of that variable's variance, suggesting the variable may not fit the factor structure well and could be considered for removal.

optWhy.A: Correct. Low communality = little variance explained by factors.
optWhy.B: High communality (near 1) indicates near-perfect measurement by factors.
optWhy.C: High loadings on all factors would be unusual and is not low communality.
optWhy.D: Sample size does not determine communality.

stem: Factor rotation is performed to:

options.text: Simplify and clarify the interpretation of factors

why: Rotation (orthogonal or oblique) reorients the factor axes to make the factor structure simpler and more interpretable (higher loadings on fewer factors per variable) without changing the underlying fit or number of factors.

optWhy.A: Correct. Rotation simplifies interpretation.
optWhy.B: Rotation does not change the number of factors.
optWhy.C: Rotation does not add variables.
optWhy.D: Rotation does not test causality.

stem: Interpreting a factor involves:

options.text: Naming it based on variables with high loadings on that factor
Using only variables with low loadings

why: A factor is interpreted/named based on the variables that load highly on it (the shared theme among those variables). Low-loading variables are not used to name it, and factors are latent constructs, not causes.

optWhy.A: Correct. Name the factor based on high-loading variables' shared theme.
optWhy.B: Low-loading variables do not define the factor.
optWhy.C: Factor loadings are essential for interpretation.
optWhy.D: Factors are latent constructs, not established causes.

stem: Before interpreting a factor solution, a researcher should verify:

options.text: KMO adequacy, significant Bartlett's, acceptable loadings and communalities

why: A defensible factor solution requires adequate sampling (KMO), significant correlations (Bartlett's), interpretable loadings, and adequate communalities. Checking only one aspect is insufficient.

optWhy.A: Correct. All these aspects must be verified.
optWhy.B: Extracting factors is not sufficient for a defensible solution.
optWhy.C: Sample size alone is insufficient.
optWhy.D: Eigenvalues alone are insufficient.

stem: One-way ANOVA: k = 3 groups, N = 15, SSB = 30, SSW = 60. The F-ratio is:

optWhy.A: Correct. F = 3.
optWhy.B: 5 is MSW, not F.
optWhy.C: 2 is dfB, not F.
optWhy.D: 4 is incorrect.

stem: Independent-samples t-test: n1 = 12, n2 = 18. Degrees of freedom =:

optWhy.A: Correct. df = 28.
optWhy.B: 29 is df for total N-1 (29) but independent t uses n1+n2-2.
optWhy.C: 30 is total N.
optWhy.D: 26 is incorrect.

stem: Two-way ANOVA: 2 x 3 design. Degrees of freedom for the interaction =:
why: df interaction = (rows-1)(cols-1) = (2-1)(3-1) = 1 x 2 = 2.

optWhy.A: Correct. df interaction = 2.
optWhy.B: 3 is cols-1 or rows, not interaction df.
optWhy.C: 1 is rows-1, not interaction df.
optWhy.D: 4 is incorrect.

stem: Repeated-measures ANOVA: n = 10 participants, k = 3 conditions. Error degrees of freedom =:

optWhy.A: Correct. df error = 18.
optWhy.B: 27 is incorrect.
optWhy.C: 9 is n-1, not error df.
optWhy.D: 20 is 2n, incorrect.

stem: One-way ANOVA: MSB = 20, MSW = 4. The F-ratio is:
why: F = MSB/MSW = 20/4 = 5.

optWhy.A: 4 is MSW, not F.
optWhy.B: Correct. F = 5.

stem: One-way ANOVA assumes:

options.text: Independence, normality, and homogeneity of variance

why: ANOVA assumes independence of observations, normality of residuals within groups, and homogeneity of variance (equal variances across groups).

optWhy.A: Correct. Independence, normality, and homogeneity of variance.
optWhy.B: Normality is necessary but not sufficient.
optWhy.C: The dependent variable should be continuous/interval, not categorical.
optWhy.D: Equal sample sizes are not required (though balanced designs are robust).

stem: A significant F-ratio in one-way ANOVA indicates:

options.text: All group means differ from each other
At least two group means differ

why: A significant F indicates that at least two group means differ (rejecting the null of all equal means). It does not specify which means differ (post-hoc tests needed) and does not establish causation.

optWhy.A: F does not indicate all means differ pairwise; post-hoc tests identify which pairs differ.
optWhy.B: Correct. Significant F means at least one pair of means differs.
optWhy.C: Significant F means at least two means differ (rejects all-equal null).
optWhy.D: ANOVA does not establish causation without experimental control.

stem: Post-hoc comparisons after ANOVA are used to:

options.text: Determine which specific group means differ after a significant F

why: Post-hoc tests (e.g., Tukey HSD) identify which specific pairs of group means differ following a significant omnibus F-test, while controlling Type I error across multiple comparisons.

optWhy.A: Correct. Post-hoc tests identify specific mean differences after a significant F.
optWhy.B: Post-hoc tests follow, not replace, the omnibus F-test.
optWhy.C: Post-hoc tests do not establish causation.
optWhy.D: Multiple comparisons increase Type I error risk; corrections reduce power.

stem: In a two-way ANOVA, a main effect concerns:

options.text: The effect of one independent variable averaged across levels of the other
The combined effect of both independent variables
Whether the effect of one IV depends on the level of the other
The correlation between the two IVs

why: A main effect is the effect of one independent variable averaged across the levels of the other independent variable. Whether the effect of one IV depends on the other is the interaction.

optWhy.A: Correct. Main effect = effect of one IV averaged across levels of the other.
optWhy.B: Combined effect is not the definition of a main effect.
optWhy.C: Whether one IV's effect depends on the other is the interaction.
optWhy.D: Correlation between IVs is multicollinearity, not a main effect.

stem: A simple effect in factorial ANOVA examines:

options.text: The effect of one IV at a single level of another IV
The overall effect of one IV across all levels of another
The correlation between the two IVs

why: A simple effect is the effect of one independent variable at a single level of another independent variable, examined when an interaction is present.

optWhy.A: Correct. Simple effect = effect of one IV at one level of another IV.
optWhy.B: The effect averaged across levels is the main effect, not simple effect.
optWhy.C: Correlation between IVs is not a simple effect.
optWhy.D: Simple effects decompose interactions but are not the interaction itself.

stem: A significant interaction in factorial ANOVA means:

options.text: The effect of one IV depends on the level of the other IV

why: A significant interaction means the effect of one independent variable on the dependent variable differs across the levels of the other independent variable (the effect is moderated).

optWhy.A: Correct. Interaction = effect of one IV depends on the level of the other.
optWhy.B: Main effects may or may not be significant independently of the interaction.
optWhy.C: Significant interaction means means are not all equal in a specific pattern.
optWhy.D: Interaction is about effects, not IV correlation.

stem: A randomised block design:

options.text: Groups participants into homogeneous blocks to reduce error variance
Assigns participants randomly to intact groups

why: A randomised block design groups homogeneous participants into blocks and randomly assigns them to treatment conditions, removing between-block variability from error to increase precision.

optWhy.A: Correct. Blocks reduce error variance by grouping homogeneous units.
optWhy.B: Measuring the same participants repeatedly is a repeated-measures design.
optWhy.C: Random assignment to intact groups is not blocking.
optWhy.D: Blocking can be used with multiple independent variables.

stem: A researcher measures the same participants before, during, and after treatment. This is:
why: Measuring the same participants on multiple occasions is a repeated-measures (within-subjects) design.

optWhy.A: Independent-measures uses different participants per condition.
optWhy.B: Correct. Same participants measured repeatedly = repeated-measures.
optWhy.C: Randomised block groups homogeneous participants, not repeated measures.
optWhy.D: Latin square controls two nuisance variables, not repeated measures per se.

stem: Counterbalancing in repeated-measures designs is used to:

options.text: Control order effects by varying the order of conditions across participants
Eliminate the need for a control group

why: Counterbalancing varies the order of conditions across participants so that order effects (practice, fatigue) are distributed evenly and do not confound the treatment effect.

optWhy.A: Correct. Counterbalancing varies order of conditions to control order effects.
optWhy.B: Counterbalancing does not increase sample size.
optWhy.C: Counterbalancing does not eliminate control groups.
optWhy.D: Counterbalancing does not prove causation.

stem: A Latin square design controls:
why: A Latin square design controls two nuisance variables simultaneously by arranging treatments so each occurs once in each row and column position.

optWhy.A: Correct. Latin square controls two nuisance variables (rows and columns).
optWhy.B: A randomised block controls one nuisance variable; Latin square controls two.
optWhy.C: Latin square controls nuisance variables, not three independent variables.
optWhy.D: Participant expectations are not the target of Latin square.

stem: A researcher has multiple correlated dependent variables. The appropriate analysis is:
why: MANOVA (multivariate ANOVA) handles multiple correlated dependent variables simultaneously, controlling Type I error and accounting for correlations among DVs. Separate ANOVAs inflate Type I error.

optWhy.A: Multiple separate ANOVAs inflate Type I error and ignore DV correlations.
optWhy.B: Correct. MANOVA handles multiple correlated DVs simultaneously.
optWhy.C: One-way ANOVA handles one DV.
optWhy.D: Chi-square tests frequencies, not continuous DVs.

stem: The purpose of a covariate in ANCOVA is to:

options.text: Adjust group means for initial differences on a related variable

why: ANCOVA adjusts group means for initial differences on a covariate (a related continuous variable), reducing error variance and controlling for pre-existing differences.

optWhy.A: Correct. Covariate adjusts group means for initial differences.
optWhy.B: A covariate does not increase groups.
optWhy.C: A covariate is not the independent variable.
optWhy.D: A covariate does not test normality.

stem: Running multiple separate ANOVAs instead of one MANOVA inflates:
why: Running multiple separate ANOVAs inflates the family-wise Type I error rate because each test carries its own alpha risk. MANOVA controls this by analysing DVs simultaneously.

optWhy.A: Correct. Multiple ANOVAs inflate family-wise Type I error.
optWhy.B: Type II error is not the primary inflation.
optWhy.C: Effect size is not inflated by multiple tests.
optWhy.D: Power is not the issue; Type I error inflation is.

stem: A researcher uses one-way ANOVA but the groups have very different variances and the data are skewed. The results are:

options.text: Compromised due to violated normality and homogeneity assumptions

why: ANOVA assumes normality and homogeneity of variance. Skewed data and very different variances violate these assumptions, compromising the validity of the F-test and p-value. A non-parametric alternative (Kruskal-Wallis) or transformation should be considered.

optWhy.A: Assumption violations compromise validity.
optWhy.B: Correct. Skewed data and unequal variances violate ANOVA assumptions.
optWhy.C: Assumption violations do not make results automatically significant.
optWhy.D: ANOVA does not prove causation.

stem: Which statements about factorial ANOVA are correct?
statements: 1. A main effect is the effect of one IV averaged across levels of the other IV.
2. An interaction is when the effect of one IV depends on the level of another IV.
3. A significant interaction means both main effects must be significant.
4. Main effects and interactions are independent concepts.
why: Statement 1 is correct (main effect = effect of one IV averaged across the other). Statement 2 is correct (interaction = effect of one IV depends on level of another). Statement 3 is incorrect: a significant interaction does not require significant main effects. Statement 4 is correct: main effects and interactions are independent concepts.

optWhy.A: Omits statement 4, which is correct.
optWhy.B: Correct. Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct; statement 3 is incorrect.
optWhy.C: Statement 3 is incorrect.
optWhy.D: Statement 3 is incorrect.

stem: Match the design (List-I) to its feature (List-II).
listII: 1. Blocks participants into homogeneous groups, different participants per condition
2. Same participants measured under all conditions
why: Randomised block design blocks participants into homogeneous groups with different participants per condition. Repeated measures uses the same participants under all conditions.

optWhy.A: Correct. A-1 (blocks, different participants), B-2 (same participants).
optWhy.B: Reverses the designs.
optWhy.C: Repeated measures is not different participants per condition.
optWhy.D: Randomised block is not same participants.

stem: An A-B-A-B design involves:

options.text: Baseline, treatment, withdrawal of treatment, reintroduction of treatment

why: An A-B-A-B (reversal) design alternates baseline (A) and treatment (B) phases twice: baseline, treatment, withdrawal of treatment, reintroduction of treatment, to demonstrate experimental control through replication.

optWhy.A: Correct. A-B-A-B = baseline, treatment, withdrawal, reintroduction.
optWhy.B: A-B is baseline-treatment only, not A-B-A-B.
optWhy.C: Multiple participants measured once is not a single-subject design.
optWhy.D: Single-subject designs do not use control groups.

stem: Visual analysis of single-subject data focuses on:

options.text: Level, trend, and variability of the data within and across phases
Only the mean of each phase

why: Visual analysis of single-subject data examines level (average responding), trend (direction of change), and variability (consistency) within and across phases to judge treatment effects.

optWhy.A: Correct. Visual analysis examines level, trend, and variability within and across phases.
optWhy.B: Mean alone is insufficient; trend and variability matter.
optWhy.C: Single-subject designs use visual analysis, not significance testing.
optWhy.D: Single-subject designs do not compare groups.

stem: A cohort study:

options.text: Follows a group of people sharing a characteristic over time
Measures different people at one time point

why: A cohort study follows a group of people who share a characteristic (e.g., birth year, exposure) over time to observe outcomes.

optWhy.A: Correct. Cohort study follows a defined group over time.
optWhy.B: Different people at one time point is cross-sectional.
optWhy.C: Random assignment is experimental, not cohort.
optWhy.D: One measurement is cross-sectional, not cohort.

stem: An interrupted time-series design evaluates:

options.text: Change in level and/or trend after an intervention, relative to the pre-intervention trend

why: Interrupted time-series measures repeated observations before and after an intervention, evaluating whether there is a change in level (immediate shift) or trend (slope) relative to the pre-intervention trajectory.

optWhy.A: Correct. Interrupted time-series evaluates level and/or trend change after intervention.
optWhy.B: Pre-intervention mean alone is insufficient.
optWhy.C: Interrupted time-series is typically single-group, not between-group.
optWhy.D: A single post-intervention measurement cannot establish trend.

stem: One-way ANOVA: k = 3 groups, N = 15, SSB = 30, SSW = 60. The F-ratio is:

optWhy.A: Correct. F = 3.
optWhy.B: 5 is MSW, not F.
optWhy.C: 2 is dfB, not F.
optWhy.D: 4 is incorrect.

stem: Pre–post differences for 5 participants: 2, 4, 3, 5, 1. The paired-samples t-statistic is approximately:

optWhy.B: 3.00 is the mean difference, not t.
optWhy.C: 2.00 underestimates t.
optWhy.D: 1.00 underestimates t.

stem: Group 1 mean = 25, Group 2 mean = 20, pooled SD = 4. Cohen's d is:
why: Cohen's d = (M1 − M2)/SD_pooled = (25 − 20)/4 = 5/4 = 1.25, a large effect.

optWhy.A: Correct. 5/4 = 1.25.
optWhy.B: 0.80 is the conventional threshold for a large effect.
optWhy.C: 5.00 is the raw mean difference.
optWhy.D: 0.20 is the conventional threshold for a small effect.

stem: If β = 0.15, the statistical power is:

optWhy.A: 0.15 is β, not power.
optWhy.B: Correct. Power = 1 − 0.15 = 0.85.
optWhy.C: 0.05 is the conventional α.
optWhy.D: 0.90 would require β = 0.10.

why: Running multiple separate ANOVAs inflates the family-wise Type I error rate because each test carries its own alpha risk. MANOVA controls this by analysing multiple dependent variables simultaneously.

optWhy.A: Correct. Multiple ANOVAs inflate family-wise Type I error.
optWhy.B: Type II error is not the primary inflation.
optWhy.C: Effect size is not inflated by multiple tests.
optWhy.D: Power is not the issue; Type I error inflation is.

stem: MANOVA assumes:

options.text: Multivariate normality, homogeneity of covariance matrices, and independence

why: MANOVA assumes multivariate normality, homogeneity of variance-covariance matrices across groups, and independence of observations.

optWhy.A: Correct. MANOVA assumes multivariate normality, homogeneity of covariance matrices, and independence.
optWhy.B: Univariate normality alone is insufficient for MANOVA.
optWhy.C: MANOVA uses continuous dependent variables.
optWhy.D: MANOVA has specific assumptions.

options.text: Adjust group means for initial differences on a related continuous variable

why: ANCOVA adjusts group means for initial differences on a covariate (a related continuous variable), reducing error variance and controlling for pre-existing differences.

optWhy.A: Correct. Covariate adjusts group means for initial differences.
optWhy.B: A covariate does not increase groups.

optWhy.D: A covariate does not test normality.

why: One continuous dependent variable and one categorical independent variable (three levels) with no covariates calls for one-way ANOVA. MANOVA requires multiple DVs; ANCOVA requires a covariate; chi-square tests frequencies.

optWhy.A: Correct. One continuous DV, one categorical IV (3 levels), no covariates = one-way ANOVA.
optWhy.B: MANOVA requires multiple dependent variables.
optWhy.C: ANCOVA requires a covariate.
optWhy.D: Chi-square tests frequencies, not continuous DVs.

optWhy.D: Multiple-baseline has multiple phases, not one.

stem: Before interpreting a factor solution, a researcher should verify:

options.text: KMO adequacy, significant Bartlett's, acceptable loadings and communalities

why: A defensible factor solution requires adequate sampling (KMO), significant correlations (Bartlett's), interpretable loadings, and adequate communalities. Checking only one aspect is insufficient.

optWhy.A: Correct. All these aspects must be verified.
optWhy.B: Extracting factors is not sufficient for a defensible solution.
optWhy.C: Sample size alone is insufficient.
optWhy.D: Eigenvalues alone are insufficient.

stem: A researcher compares anxiety across three independent clinics using ordinal ratings with skewed distributions and unequal clinic sizes. The appropriate analysis is:
why: Three independent groups, ordinal data, skewed distributions, and unequal sizes violate one-way ANOVA assumptions. The Kruskal–Wallis H test is the non-parametric alternative for k independent groups.

optWhy.A: One-way ANOVA requires interval/ratio data, normality, and homogeneity of variance.
optWhy.B: Correct. Kruskal–Wallis H suits ordinal, skewed, independent k-group data.
optWhy.C: Paired-samples t is for two related groups.
optWhy.D: Pearson r measures correlation.

stem: Statistical power and effect size differ in that:

options.text: Power depends on effect size, sample size, and alpha; effect size is independent of sample size
Power and effect size are identical
Power increases as effect size decreases
Effect size depends on sample size

why: Power depends on effect size, sample size, alpha, and variability. Effect size is a property of the relationship and is independent of sample size.

optWhy.A: Correct. Power depends on effect size, sample size, and alpha; effect size is independent of sample size.
optWhy.B: Power and effect size are distinct concepts.
optWhy.C: Power increases as effect size increases, not decreases.
optWhy.D: Effect size is independent of sample size.

optWhy.A: One-way ANOVA requires interval/ratio data, normality, and homogeneity of variance.

stem: A significant correlation between two variables does not imply causation because:

options.text: A third variable may explain the association

why: A correlation between two variables may reflect a third variable influencing both (common cause), rather than one causing the other. Correlation alone cannot establish causation.

optWhy.A: Correct. A third variable (common cause) may explain the association.
optWhy.B: Correlation does not imply causation.
optWhy.C: Sample size does not resolve causation.
optWhy.D: A significant correlation means the variables are related.

stem: A researcher studying a sensitive topic must especially attend to:

options.text: Informed consent, confidentiality, and emotional risk

why: Sensitive topics require careful attention to informed consent, confidentiality, and emotional/psychological risk to participants.

optWhy.A: Random assignment is an experimental procedure.
optWhy.B: Correct. Informed consent, confidentiality, and emotional risk are key ethical concerns.
optWhy.C: Statistical power is quantitative.
optWhy.D: Standardisation is not the primary ethical concern.

stem: A researcher wants both to measure the prevalence of a behaviour and understand why it occurs. The most suitable paradigm is:
why: Measuring prevalence is quantitative; understanding why is qualitative. Mixed methods combines both.

optWhy.A: Quantitative only measures prevalence but cannot explain why.
optWhy.B: Qualitative only explains why but cannot measure prevalence.
optWhy.C: Correct. Mixed methods addresses both prevalence (quant) and why (qual).
optWhy.D: Case study only is too narrow for prevalence measurement.

stem: A researcher wants to test a theory quantitatively and explore participants' lived experiences, giving equal priority to both. The best design is:
why: Equal priority to quantitative theory-testing and qualitative exploration, collected and analysed separately then merged, is a convergent mixed-methods design with equal priority.

optWhy.A: Explanatory sequential is quant first then qual, not equal priority in parallel.
optWhy.B: Exploratory sequential is qual first then quant, not equal priority in parallel.
optWhy.C: Correct. Equal priority quantitative + qualitative, merged, is convergent mixed-methods.
optWhy.D: Purely quantitative omits the lived-experience strand.

stem: A researcher compares anxiety across three independent clinics using ordinal ratings with skewed distributions and unequal clinic sizes, and also wants to adjust for baseline anxiety. The appropriate analysis is:
why: Three independent groups, ordinal data, skewed distributions violate ANOVA assumptions. ANCOVA requires interval/ratio covariates. Kruskal–Wallis H is the appropriate non-parametric test for k independent ordinal groups.

optWhy.A: One-way ANOVA requires interval/ratio data, normality, and homogeneity.
optWhy.B: Correct. Kruskal–Wallis H suits ordinal, skewed, independent k-group data.
optWhy.C: ANCOVA requires interval/ratio data and a covariate.
optWhy.D: Pearson r measures correlation.
